opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the analogy fits pretty well if you look at where people ended up. Around 2022 and into early 2023, Google had what was probably the densest concentration of robot learning talent anywhere in the world. You had the robotics team inside Google Brain, later folded into DeepMind, and you also had Everyday Robots over at X, which was trying to build general-purpose mobile manipulators for real environments like offices.

Inside that group, a lot of the ideas that now define the field were being worked out: large-scale data collection on real robots, putting transformers on robot control, the RT series of models, and SayCan, which connected large language models to robot actions. So the people there weren't just good engineers. They had lived through the whole transition from narrow, hand-engineered robotics to the idea that you could train something like a foundation model for the physical world.

Then early 2023 hit. There were big layoffs across Google, Everyday Robots was wound down, and the industry was going through a reorganization after ChatGPT. Many of these researchers suddenly had a clear thesis, a lot of hands-on experience, and a reason to leave. At the same time, investors were excited about what large models could do and were asking what the next frontier would be. Embodied AI was an obvious answer.

So over the next year or two you saw a wave of startups whose founding teams or key early people came out of that Google lineage, in the US and also among Chinese researchers who went back home or started companies elsewhere. That's why I call it the Whampoa Military Academy. Like the original Whampoa, it wasn't just one institution producing a few famous names. It trained a whole generation of officers who shared a common doctrine, then scattered and each led their own army. In robotics, the shared doctrine was basically: scale data, use large models, and aim for generality rather than solving one task at a time.

One more point: Google itself didn't capture most of the commercial value from that period. It funded the research and trained the people, but because of how big companies prioritize, the momentum ended up flowing out into the startup ecosystem. That's part of what makes the analogy feel right to me.

fable-5.1.text:
I use that phrase because of how many robotics founders came out of one place in a very short window. If you look at the wave of embodied AI startups that formed in early 2023, a striking number of the founding teams trace back to Google's research org, specifically Google Brain, Everyday Robots, and the robotics group that produced work like SayCan, RT-1, and PaLM-E.

Whampoa was the academy that trained a whole generation of officers who then went out and led armies on different sides. That's the dynamic I saw. Google had spent years assembling the people, the data, and the compute to show that large models could actually drive robots in the real world. Then, right around the time ChatGPT landed, Google shut down Everyday Robots and reorganized Brain into DeepMind. Suddenly you had a few hundred people who had seen firsthand that the foundation-model approach worked for robotics, and many of them no longer had a clear home inside the company.

So they scattered. Some went to build general-purpose robot foundation models, some went into humanoids, some into manipulation startups, some into data companies. Physical Intelligence, Skild, and several others have deep Google lineage. Many had worked on the same projects, shared the same intuitions about scaling, and even disagreed with each other in the same way classmates do about which path is right.

That's why I call it the academy. It wasn't that Google invented robotics startups. It was that one institution concentrated the talent and the conviction, and then released it all at once into the market at exactly the moment capital decided embodied AI was the next frontier.

r003.rationale: The response links Google shutting down Everyday Robots and reorganizing Brain to researchers losing a clear home, scattering, and forming robotics startups.

astra-6.text:
I use “Whampoa Military Academy” as a metaphor for a training ground for founders. Google brought together people working on robotics, machine learning, perception, and control, and gave them the resources to tackle difficult problems together. That experience built both technical expertise and relationships that could later become the foundation of startup teams.

So, looking at the robotics startup landscape in early 2023, the point is less about one particular Google product and more about its influence through people. Researchers can leave a large organization, take what they learned, and pursue a focused commercial opportunity. In that sense, a research organization can become an incubator for an entire generation of companies.

sol-6.1.text:
What I mean by “Whampoa Military Academy” is that Google trained and brought together a large pool of robotics talent, and many of those people later became founders or core team members at startups. It’s an analogy about where people were trained and the networks they formed.

Robotics research requires substantial resources: hardware, computing, and time to explore ideas that may not immediately become products. Google gave researchers an environment to develop that experience and work with strong colleagues. When they left to start companies, they took that technical judgment and those relationships with them.

So, looking at the startup landscape in early 2023, Google’s influence extended beyond its own robotics projects. You could also see it in the people building the next generation of robotics companies.
